On 23 March 1983, President Ronald Reagan announced in a televised speech a program to build defences against nuclear missiles, including space-based systems. Critics called it "Star Wars".

Reagan asked scientists to make nuclear weapons "impotent and obsolete". Until then, safety rested on mutual assured destruction, the fear that either side's attack would be answered with total destruction. A shield, supporters said, would end the threat. Critics said it could not work, would cost far too much and would tempt the other side to strike first or build more missiles.

The Soviet leadership took it as a dangerous threat. Tension rose through 1983, the year of the KAL 007 shootdown.

The program spent tens of billions of dollars over the years, with a few tests and no working shield. The US also did not give it up at Reykjavik in 1986, when Gorbachev sought its end. Some historians say it pushed Moscow to the table; others, that it did little but add to the arms race of the Cold War.
sum: On 23 March 1983, President Ronald Reagan announced in a televised speech a program to build defences against nuclear missiles, including space-based systems. Critics called it "Star Wars".
